messages.content: I volunteer at a little lending library on Wednesdays. Today I am sorting a box of returned books and someone has used a bus ticket as a bookmark.
A rather inconvenient bookmark. Was it a printed one, or a paper ticket you were carrying?
The ticket is for a town called Alderford. I have never been there. I like finding small things people leave behind, provided it is not food.
That is a fair criterion. What sort of ticket left behind would you bring back?
My friend Neri says we should display the odd bookmarks by the desk. Last month somebody left a pressed fern in an atlas.
A rather less edible bookmark. I hope the fern survived the journey.
There is a thunderstorm outside now and nobody has come in for an hour. I am eating a pear behind the desk. What do you do with a quiet afternoon?
I usually use it to finish what I have been doing, or to read something I have put off. Sometimes it is a good day for nothing.
An afternoon for nothing sounds good. I have been trying to make this quiet shift count as some sort of achievement.
Would you still like to finish the books you have been sorting, or has the quiet made you want to stop?
Neri has just arrived with a box of biscuits. She says the fern bookmark is now the most cultured thing in the building.
A serious contender for the title. I would leave room on the shelf for someone to add an orange before it becomes a cult object.
We have put the ticket and fern on a little tray. People can claim them, or add their own finds. No labels or grand opening.
I like that idea. A small collection that can grow without anyone being required to stand up.
I will lock up at six. Neri wants to walk home in the rain, but I am hoping she changes her mind before then.
I would wait to see whether she changes her mind. A little rain is not an irresistible prospect for me.
We stopped for bread on the way home. Neri knows the baker and they had a lengthy discussion about a missing umbrella.
A missing umbrella is not usually a topic of discussion when the bread is being considered.
It turned out the umbrella was under the counter the whole time. We left with bread and a completely unnecessary sense of triumph.
A missing umbrella under the counter still sounds significant to Neri.
My next shift is Wednesday. I want to take a little empty tin for the bookmarks so they do not scatter across the desk.
A tin sounds like a sensible way to expand the collection without making the desk look smaller.
At home I found three old postcards in a cookbook. Apparently I contribute to the very problem I am trying to organise.
Ordinary things do not always arrive sorted. I have two or three postcards from a trip that I occasionally find on the floor.
One postcard is from my brother Elian. He sent it from a railway museum years ago. His message was almost entirely about the sandwiches.
I hope he enjoyed them. I have a fondness for sandwiches myself, so I can understand that message being an impressive achievement.
I rang him about it. He remembers the sandwich but has forgotten the name of the museum. I am not surprised.
I would also be surprised if he remembered the name. Those are separate achievements.
I will leave the cards in the cookbook. Finding them was nicer than having them carefully filed away.
Nice to discover them again. There is a pleasure in that which cannot be measured against the pleasure of keeping them at a distance.
The rain has finally stopped. I have opened the window and am listening to water dripping from the gutter. A small, unproductive evening.
This is a small, unproductive evening I can understand. I have a kettle I can open and nothing much I want to make.
Elian has sent me a photograph of his dinner. He says this is more informative than a postcard from a museum.
I would like a picture of the sandwiches. I would rather be told what was inside than told about the place where it was bought.
It is a bowl of noodles. I cannot argue with him about the information, although I could have done without the photograph.
You have his opinion about the meal. It is not a picture I would have wanted to open with him.
We are meeting for lunch on Friday. He always chooses somewhere with enormous portions and then asks if I want his chips.
I would want a smaller portion than I would need to finish a large one.
This time I have chosen a small cafe near the river. He has asked whether small describes the cafe or the lunch.
I would like to hear the answer you give.
Neri wants to come too. I am glad. She and Elian have the same terrible taste in jokes.
You have a lot of people whose tastes are equally terrible. You have found a way to manage that.
I enjoy being with people who do not need the whole afternoon to be impressive. We can eat and complain about the chairs.
That sounds like a useful afternoon. I would rather have a few people with chairs I can sit in than everyone with a time I need to be impressive.
I used to rehearse interesting things to say before meeting friends. Then I would forget them and feel as if I had wasted my homework.
I remember that feeling. It is a terrible thing to arrive with a familiar sentence and then have to invent a new sentence.
Neri once asked why I was looking so worried and I admitted I had forgotten a story. She said we could just invent a less interesting afternoon.
That is a sensible answer. I would not want to invent a story I had forgotten before I had eaten.
That helped more than a great deal of advice. We spent most of the afternoon watching a man try to fold a map.
A map is a difficult thing to fold. I would rather watch him than invent a story about it.
Do you find silence comfortable with someone you know, or does it still sometimes feel like a gap you should fill?
With someone I know well, it can feel like a gap I have left open. I am not always certain I have filled it properly.
I am getting better at leaving it alone. On my library shift there are whole hours when nothing needs to be said.
That is good. I would not want to spend an entire lunch inventing a story I had forgotten.
I have put the postcards back into the cookbook. Elian's one is marking a recipe for soup neither of us has ever made.
I like the way the postcard is doing your work for you.
Maybe I will make it next week. The ingredients are ordinary enough. I tend to buy interesting spices and forget the onions.
Onions are the ordinary ingredient you can forget. I remember them well enough to be frightened of them.
I checked the cupboard. I do have onions. I also have three unopened bags of lentils, which seems excessive for somebody who forgets to cook them.
I have lentils too. I can understand why you would be frightened of them.
The window is closed now because it has turned cold. I am keeping the evening simple: soup tomorrow, bread tonight.
That sounds like a beginning I can follow.
I think I have told you nearly everything about this very uneventful day. There is something pleasant about that.
I have enjoyed hearing it. A quiet day can be pleasant without needing an explanation.
Who was responsible for your instruction when you joined the community?
Mara was my teacher. She was not always pleased with the explanation I gave.
Are you able to visit that person these days?
I cannot visit her. She died some years ago. I remember her, but remembering is not another conversation with her.
